quiz.title: Chapter 13 Quiz: Dockets and Court Documents
quiz.intro: Ten questions on what a docket holds, when to open one, and why a brief is a lead rather than an answer.

items.q: The first discipline of this chapter is:
options: Court documents are research tools, not a source of authority
items.why: A brief tells you what one party argued, not what the law is (chapter opening; Court Documents and the Research Cycle).

items.q: Why does the method send you to dockets only after your question has narrowed?
options: Because early exploratory questions are answered by secondary sources; a brief becomes a shortcut only once a focusing or application question is in front of you
Because court documents are secondary sources
items.why: Reaching for PACER before you know the governing standard wastes money and time (Court Documents and the Research Cycle).

items.q: A docket find should be reframed as:
options: A new research question: does the authority this brief cites actually say what the brief claims?
items.why: Running that verification is the cycle continuing, not concluding (Court Documents and the Research Cycle).

items.q: Which documents does the chapter say are most worth locating on a docket?
options: The complaint, the dispositive motions with their briefs, and the court’s orders resolving those motions
items.why: Do not confuse docket entries with the documents themselves; you have to open each entry (Understanding a Docket).

options: Is free and hosts the RECAP archive of PACER documents uploaded by users
items.why: PACER is comprehensive but metered, with a quarterly waiver threshold (Finding a Docket).

items.q: What does the Mata v. Avianca docket hold that the published decision does not?
options: How the failure unfolded: the order to show cause, the affidavit, the hearing transcript, and the letters the court required
The fabricated cases themselves as real law
items.why: That is the part that answers “how do I keep this from happening in my office?” (Example: What only the docket holds).

items.q: Complaints are most useful for answering:
options: What the full range of arguments on an issue is
How lawyers have framed similar legal theories
How the court reasoned through procedural issues
items.why: Briefs answer the range of arguments, amicus briefs the non-party perspectives, orders the court’s procedural reasoning (Answering Questions with Court Documents).

items.q: The court rules hierarchy to work through before filing is:
options: Federal Rules, then local court rules, then judge-specific standing orders
items.why: A perfectly researched motion filed in violation of a local formatting rule can still be rejected (Court Rules Research).
They explain why a rule was written as it was (Court Rules Research).

items.q: Searching dockets for pending cases on your issue can reveal:
options: That the law is about to change, sometimes before any citator flag appears
items.why: Always check whether a leading case has been granted certiorari or is on appeal (Pending Cases).

drills.blurb: Eight research needs. Which court document answers each, and which need the docket cannot meet at all?
